paragraphs: Fonts pose a difficult representation problem: their shapes include sharp corners and edges that must remain crisp. Native vector formats do not fit easily into common neural representation architectures, while encoding rasterized images can lose these details. This paper develops a neural representation designed to preserve those distinctive geometric features.

The approach builds a complex glyph from several simpler occupancy functions, which describe which locations belong to a shape. These learned functions form a set whose ordering does not matter. Combining multiple functions lets the representation preserve local features without requiring a single neural function to capture every sharp transition.

Training creates another challenge because separate ground-truth signals for those functions are not readily available. The authors instead use local supervision and an architecture that finds globally consistent functions across font families. Evaluations on reconstruction, interpolation, and synthesis show advantages over existing alternatives. The representation also supports glyph completion, using a single characteristic font example to synthesize a family in the target style.
neurips-2021-a-multi-implicit-neural-rep.tldr: A set of learned implicit functions represents fonts while preserving sharp features and supporting reconstruction, synthesis, and glyph completion.

paragraphs: This paper asks how large a deep threshold network must be to memorize labeled data. The relevant quantities are the number of points n, their dimension d, and their minimum separation δ. Earlier bounds had an exponential dependence on inverse separation, making the stated sufficient network size grow rapidly as points became closer.

The authors construct networks with a much milder dependence on separation. Up to logarithmic factors, they show that 1/δ + √n neurons and d/δ + n weights are sufficient. These are upper bounds on resources needed for memorization, rather than claims that every dataset requires networks of exactly those sizes.

The construction also restricts where complicated weights are needed: only the first layer uses Gaussian random weights, while later layers use binary or integer weights. Alongside these upper bounds, the paper proves new lower bounds by connecting memorization to separating points on a sphere with hyperplanes. Together, the results sharpen the relationship between dataset geometry and network memorization capacity.
neurips-2021-an-exponential-improvement-.tldr: A new construction greatly reduces the sufficient size of deep threshold networks for memorization, replacing exponential separation dependence with nearly linear dependence.

paragraphs: A weighted majority vote combines predictions from several models, giving some models more influence than others. This paper develops a new bound on its expected prediction risk. The bound uses second-order information and is designed to address both the quality of the guarantee and the difficulty of optimizing it.

The first contribution is a parameterized version of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality, which controls deviations in one direction. Its form permits efficient minimization, resolving an optimization obstacle in earlier bounds known as C-bounds. The resulting oracle bound also improves on a previous bound derived from the second-order Markov inequality.

To estimate that oracle bound from data, the authors introduce PAC-Bayes-Bennett, combining PAC-Bayesian reasoning with Bennett's concentration inequality. They show that it improves on an earlier PAC-Bayes-Bernstein inequality. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that the new bounds can improve on prior work, rather than establishing improvement in every setting. Both mathematical inequalities may also prove useful for studying concentration outside weighted voting.
neurips-2021-chebyshev-cantelli-pac-baye.tldr: New concentration inequalities provide improved, efficiently optimizable risk bounds for weighted majority votes.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning causal relationships across multiple independent entities, each with its own causal graph. Learning every graph separately can require many experiments. The central question is whether shared structure across entities can reduce the experimental effort while still recovering each entity's individual causal relationships.

The framework allows hidden causes rather than assuming that all relevant causal variables are observed. It represents relationships using Maximal Ancestral Graphs and assumes access to atomic interventions: experiments that intervene on one observable variable at a time, independently for the different entities. These assumptions define the kind of causal discovery problem addressed.

When the M underlying graphs satisfy a specified clustering property, the proposed algorithms exploit that structure to recover all graphs using roughly logarithmically many interventions in M per entity. The abstract contrasts this with n interventions per entity for learning graphs separately, where n counts observable nodes. A lower bound and extensions complement the algorithms. The intervention savings therefore depend on the stated shared clustering structure.
neurips-2021-collaborative-causal-discov.tldr: Under a clustering assumption, collaboratively learning causal graphs can substantially reduce the atomic interventions required per entity.

paragraphs: Constrained Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions while respecting feasibility requirements. A method focused only on immediate improvement may avoid the boundary between feasible and infeasible regions. The authors argue that this caution can delay discovery of excellent solutions near tight constraints, making planning beyond the next evaluation especially valuable.

Their method, 2-OPT-C, evaluates the value of looking two steps ahead and supports both sequential and batch queries. The computational challenge is that constraints create discontinuities in sampled acquisition functions. These discontinuities prevent efficient derivative techniques used for unconstrained lookahead optimization from carrying over directly to this setting.

The paper develops an unbiased gradient estimator based on likelihood ratios, enabling fast optimization without the reparameterization trick. This connects a longer planning horizon with a practical way to choose evaluations. In numerical experiments, the method typically improves query efficiency by at least a factor of two over previous methods, with improvements of tenfold or more in some cases. Those gains are reported experimental outcomes.
neurips-2021-constrained-two-step-look-a.tldr: An efficient two-step lookahead method improves constrained Bayesian optimization by accounting for future evaluations and estimating gradients despite constraint discontinuities.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems can benefit from learning auxiliary predictions about their environment. Existing off-policy algorithms can learn such predictions from collected experience, but they leave another question: how should the agent act to gather experience that improves those predictions? This paper makes that data-collection behavior part of the learning problem.

The proposed system learns a collection of auxiliary tasks while also learning a behavior policy whose actions aim to improve them. This creates non-stationarity on both sides. The prediction learners operate within an evolving system, and the behavior learner must adapt as the usefulness of different experiences changes during learning.

The authors develop an algorithm based on successor features to support tracking when rewards change. Its structure separates learning successor features from learning rewards, and they prove that this separation improves convergence rates. An in-depth study examines the resulting system of multiple predictions and learned behavior. The contribution links auxiliary learning with active experience collection, treating both as interacting parts of a continual learning process.
neurips-2021-continual-auxiliary-task-le.tldr: A successor-feature approach learns both auxiliary predictions and behavior that gathers useful experience, with convergence-rate benefits from separating features and rewards.

paragraphs: Transferring a visual reinforcement learning policy from simulation to reality often requires aligning simulated and real images. That can make simulation expensive because it must produce high-quality visual output. This paper considers a cheaper setup: simulate only compact states, while the deployed agent receives images from the target environment.

The challenge is then alignment across different kinds of observations. The authors argue that earlier representation-matching objectives are ill-posed: they can produce an incorrect correspondence even when representations appear aligned. They find that crossing modalities makes this failure more likely. CODAS addresses the ambiguity by using the sequential structure of experience collected during reinforcement learning.

That temporal structure supplies information beyond matching observations individually, helping constrain the learned correspondence. Experiments on MuJoCo and Hand Manipulation Suite tasks show deployed agents performing similarly to their source-domain performance. Earlier methods designed for alignment within the same modality exhibit larger performance gaps. These results support the proposed route to transfer without requiring a simulator that renders high-quality images.
neurips-2021-cross-modal-domain-adaptati.tldr: CODAS uses sequential experience to align simulated compact states with visual observations, reducing the need for costly image-rendering simulators.

paragraphs: Generating images under specified conditions usually requires examples connecting those conditions to images, and those labels can be expensive. D2C approaches the problem by first training an unconditional variational autoencoder. The aim is to learn an image model that can later adapt to new conditional generation tasks with relatively little supervision.

Two ingredients strengthen this starting model. A learned diffusion prior models its latent representations to improve generation, while contrastive self-supervised learning improves representation quality. The model can then learn tasks specified through labels or image-manipulation constraints using as few as 100 labeled examples, as reported in the abstract.

For generation from new labels, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art variational autoencoders and diffusion models. For conditional image manipulation, they report generation roughly 100 times faster than StyleGAN2 and preference from 50–60% of human evaluators in a double-blind study. These findings connect the learned representation and generative prior to adaptation efficiency, generation speed, and evaluated output quality.
neurips-2021-d2c-diffusion-decoding-mode.tldr: D2C combines a diffusion latent prior with contrastive representations to adapt image generation to new conditions using few labeled examples.

paragraphs: The cold posterior effect occurs when a Bayesian neural network predicts better after its posterior is artificially sharpened using a temperature below one. This is puzzling because it changes the usual Bayesian posterior. The paper investigates three proposed explanations: dataset curation, data augmentation, and the choice of prior.

The curation results resist a simple explanation. The effect is absent in one real curated dataset, yet appears in a controlled experiment that varies curation strength. For augmentation, the experiments show that it can be sufficient to produce the effect but is not necessary: the effect can also occur without augmentation.

A separate experiment compares the influence of prior and likelihood and strongly links the effect to the prior. Taken together, the findings indicate that synthetic curation, augmentation, and problematic priors can each contribute in isolation. The authors therefore argue that cold posteriors encountered in practice are unlikely to have a single simple cause. Their evidence motivates distinguishing these mechanisms rather than expecting one universal correction.
neurips-2021-disentangling-the-roles-of-.tldr: Experiments separate several contributors to the cold posterior effect and argue against a single-cause explanation or simple universal fix.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from multiple devices into a shared model. Poisoned updates can corrupt that model, and the authors observe that their effects can persist even after attacks stop. They also find that existing server-side defenses can fail under extremely strong attacks, motivating recovery measures on participating clients.

FL-WBC identifies the region of parameter space associated with persistent attack effects and perturbs it during local training. Its goal is to reduce damage that has already entered the shared model. The paper derives a certified robustness guarantee against model poisoning and a convergence guarantee to FedAvg after applying the defense.

Experiments on FashionMNIST and CIFAR10 evaluate defenses against state-of-the-art poisoning attacks. The authors report effective mitigation within five communication rounds with almost no accuracy loss, under both identically distributed and heterogeneous client data. They also show that FL-WBC complements robust aggregation at the server. The findings support combining client-side repair with server-side defenses to improve robustness in the evaluated attack settings.
neurips-2021-fl-wbc-enhancing-robustness.tldr: FL-WBC perturbs client-side parameters associated with persistent poisoning effects to help repair corrupted federated models and complement server defenses.

paragraphs: Matching markets often unfold over several stages without a single central decision maker. Participants also face uncertainty about preferences and acceptance. This paper develops a framework for learning strategies in that setting, where a participant's choices must account for both potential payoff and uncertainty about whether a match will occur.

The approach combines nonparametric statistical methods with variational analysis. Its efficient algorithm uses concepts called a lower uncertainty bound and calibrated decentralized matching to maximize expected payoff. The analysis identifies a trade-off between welfare and fairness whose character depends on uncertainty about acceptance, making that uncertainty central to market behavior.

The authors show that participants strategically favor lower uncertainty to reduce competition and increase expected payoff. They also prove that participants can benefit from having multiple matching stages compared with a single stage; this is a possibility result rather than a claim that everyone always benefits. Simulations and an experiment using college-admissions data demonstrate aspects of the theoretical predictions, connecting the framework to an applied matching setting.
neurips-2021-learning-in-multi-stage-dec.tldr: A learning framework for decentralized matching links acceptance uncertainty to strategic behavior, welfare–fairness trade-offs, and possible benefits from multiple stages.

paragraphs: Requesting a human label can do more than create training data: it can also finish the task for that example. In spam detection, for instance, a reviewer may already make the needed decision. The machine consequently handles a different set of examples depending on which ones were sent for labeling.

This paper formalizes that connection between label collection and machine responsibility. It introduces an algorithm that jointly learns a prediction model and decides when to request labels. The approach combines active learning, which selects informative examples for labeling, with abstention, which allows the machine to leave some decisions to another resource.

The authors prove an upper bound on label complexity and a matching lower bound for any algorithm in the formalized setting. This establishes a theoretical benchmark for how much labeling is needed. Experiments, including an ablation study, examine the algorithm's components. An efficient version outperforms margin sampling across multiple datasets, supporting the usefulness of explicitly accounting for how labeling changes the examples left for automation.
neurips-2021-learning-with-labeling-indu.tldr: A joint learning-and-labeling algorithm accounts for human-labeled examples no longer needing machine prediction, with matching label-complexity bounds.

paragraphs: Some learning and inverse problems require a finite set of points that represents a target probability distribution. One approach assigns equal probability to N points and adjusts their locations to minimize Wasserstein distance from the target. The optimization is non-convex and can contain spurious critical points, making practical success theoretically surprising.

The paper analyzes an adjusted Lloyd algorithm that replaces Voronoi cells with Power cells. Although this procedure often produces low-error configurations, non-convexity makes its convergence behavior difficult to explain. The authors provide explicit bounds on convergence speed when the starting points are sufficiently separated from one another.

The bounds already apply after a single iteration, and related bounds follow for the corresponding gradient descent procedure. They also yield a form of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality for the Wasserstein objective, including an error term determined by distances between the discrete point masses. The result provides finite-iteration control under a concrete geometric starting condition, helping explain why useful approximation can occur despite the optimization landscape's difficulties.
neurips-2021-non-asymptotic-convergence-.tldr: Explicit convergence bounds explain Wasserstein point-cloud approximation by a Lloyd-type algorithm when its initial points are sufficiently separated.

paragraphs: Local implicit functions can represent large three-dimensional scenes, but regularly dividing all of space allocates resources inefficiently. Much of the volume may contain no surface, while different surface regions need different detail levels. The paper identifies this mismatch as a source of rapidly growing memory and computational costs.

OctField uses an adaptive octree hierarchy to place local implicit functions around relevant surfaces. It subdivides space according to both surface occupancy and geometric complexity. This allows intricate regions to receive finer representation while avoiding the same dense subdivision everywhere, supporting precise surface encoding with a low memory and computation budget.

Learning the hierarchy introduces a difficulty because discrete octree subdivisions are not differentiable. The authors address it with a hierarchical network that treats subdivision probabilistically and recursively encodes and decodes both structure and geometry in a differentiable way. Evaluations across shape modeling and reconstruction tasks show advantages over alternative approaches. The contribution joins adaptive spatial allocation with a learnable representation of the surface itself.
neurips-2021-octfield-hierarchical-impli.tldr: OctField learns an adaptive octree of local implicit functions to represent detailed 3D surfaces with reduced memory and computation.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations are often used to explain the behavior of stochastic gradient descent in deep networks. A central concern is that existing formal justifications apply to very small learning rates, while finite learning rates matter for practical generalization. Directly checking the approximation has also appeared computationally impractical.

The paper introduces SVAG, an efficient simulation algorithm that provably converges to the conventional Itô stochastic differential equation approximation. This provides a practical way to examine the continuous-time model. The authors also derive a theoretically motivated, testable necessary condition for the approximation and its associated linear scaling rule to hold.

A necessary condition can help identify when an explanation fails, but satisfying it alone does not establish that the approximation is valid. Experiments using the simulator show that the previously proposed equation can meaningfully capture training and generalization properties of common deep networks. The work therefore contributes both a tool for testing the approximation and empirical evidence that it can remain informative beyond the tiny-learning-rate regime.
neurips-2021-on-the-validity-of-modeling.tldr: SVAG makes a standard continuous-time model of SGD testable, while experiments show it can capture training and generalization in common deep networks.

paragraphs: Kernel regression may be trained on one distribution and evaluated on another, making prediction performance difficult to anticipate. This paper uses tools from statistical physics to study that mismatch. Through the replica method, the authors derive an analytical expression for out-of-distribution generalization error that applies to arbitrary kernels and real datasets.

A key object is an overlap matrix that measures distribution mismatch in a way specific to the chosen kernel. This makes the relationship between the kernel and the shift central to the analysis. The expressions explain several phenomena, including the possibility that a training–test mismatch can improve generalization rather than necessarily making it worse.

The authors also develop procedures to optimize training and test distributions under a fixed data budget, identifying favorable and unfavorable shifts. Applications cover synthetic and real datasets with multiple kernels, alongside a deeper analysis of linear regression. For the Neural Tangent Kernel, theoretical predictions agree with simulations of wide networks, connecting the kernel analysis to that neural-network setting.
neurips-2021-out-of-distribution-general.tldr: A statistical-physics analysis characterizes kernel regression under distribution shift and explains why some mismatches can improve generalization.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can require substantial task-specific experience. This paper studies whether an encoder can first learn useful representations from unlabeled data and then be fine-tuned using a small amount of experience for a particular task. The goal is to make the later learning stage more data efficient.

Pretraining combines latent dynamics modeling with unsupervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. These components encourage the representation to capture diverse aspects of the underlying decision process. The encoder is therefore trained through both modeling changes in its latent space and learning behavior conditioned on goals, before task-specific fine-tuning begins.

With task interaction limited to 100,000 steps on Atari games, the approach significantly outperforms earlier work combining offline representation pretraining and fine-tuning. It also compares favorably with other pretraining approaches that use orders of magnitude more data. Larger models and more diverse observations aligned with the task show particular promise. In the authors' best setting, performance and data efficiency approach human levels on Atari; that qualification matters to the reported result.
neurips-2021-pretraining-representations.tldr: Unlabeled pretraining that combines latent dynamics and goal-conditioned learning improves Atari reinforcement learning with limited task-specific interaction.

paragraphs: Participatory budgeting lets voters choose projects to fund from a shared budget. This paper allows projects to have different costs and voters to assign arbitrary additive values to them. The fairness question is how to give groups with shared interests proportional representation when neither project prices nor voter valuations are uniform.

The authors formulate two axioms expressing that representation requirement. They report that, to their knowledge, existing participatory-budgeting rules satisfy neither. They also show that Proportional Approval Voting, a prominent rule for committee elections, cannot be adapted to arbitrary costs or additive valuations in a way that satisfies their proposed proportionality axioms.

The constructive results distinguish what is efficiently achievable from what needs a more demanding procedure. A simple rule satisfies one axiom for arbitrary costs and additive valuations and can be computed in polynomial time. The stronger axiom is also achievable, but through a more computationally expensive and less natural rule. The paper thus supplies explicit fairness criteria and voting procedures with different computational requirements.
neurips-2021-proportional-participatory-.tldr: New proportionality axioms for participatory budgeting lead to an efficient voting rule and a more expensive rule satisfying a stronger guarantee.

paragraphs: Research on the lottery ticket hypothesis has used inconsistent experimental setups and criteria for identifying a winning ticket. This paper revisits the definition and introduces more comprehensive, rigorous conditions. Its purpose is to make claims about winning tickets easier to assess across neural-network architectures and applications.

Using those conditions, the authors conduct extensive experiments and analyze how identification of winning tickets relates to experimental choices. Learning rate and training duration are strongly correlated with whether and when a ticket can be identified. Architectural properties, including model capacity and residual connections, also show strong correlations with those outcomes.

These findings make the experimental setup part of the interpretation of a winning-ticket result. They are reported correlations, rather than a claim that one setting universally determines success. Based on the observed patterns, the authors provide guidance for choosing parameters in light of architectural characteristics. The contribution combines clearer evaluation criteria with empirical evidence about which factors accompany successful identification across the settings studied.
neurips-2021-sanity-checks-for-lottery-t.tldr: Stricter winning-ticket criteria reveal strong correlations between ticket identification, training choices, and neural-network architecture.

paragraphs: Answering questions over a knowledge graph can require following several relationships and applying more complex logical constraints. Many existing methods scale with the graph's edge count, restricting effective use to small, question-specific subgraphs. SQALER addresses this computational obstacle by separating multi-hop reasoning from the more complex logical reasoning stage.

The paper shows that this separation can preserve expressive power. Its multi-hop method scales linearly with the number of relation types, a quantity usually much smaller than the number of graph nodes or edges. It produces candidate answers that can then be refined, with a proof that the refinement recovers the original problem's solution.

Experiments show that the approach solves the multi-hop MetaQA dataset and establishes a new state of the art on WebQuestionsSP. The authors also report scalability improvements of orders of magnitude over competitive methods. Their results demonstrate that compositional generalization beyond the training distribution is possible. The central contribution is a reasoning decomposition that combines a smaller scaling variable with a principled route to final answers.
neurips-2021-sqaler-scaling-question-ans.tldr: SQALER separates multi-hop search from logical refinement to scale knowledge-graph question answering while preserving expressive power.

paragraphs: Quantum kernels can compute similarities involving extremely large quantum representations, but that capability alone does not establish a learning advantage. Classical kernels can also represent high- or infinite-dimensional feature spaces. Moreover, very large function spaces make generalization difficult, so computational access to those spaces is only part of the problem.

The authors analyze quantum-kernel spectra and identify a promising conditional setting: a low-dimensional function space containing functions that are hard to compute classically. If the target is known to belong to this space, the quantum model can encode a useful inductive bias that cannot be imposed efficiently in the same way classically.

Constructing such kernels remains difficult because evaluating them may require exponentially many measurements. The authors conjecture that quantum learning speedups require encoding problem knowledge into circuits when encoding the same bias classically is hard. They suggest that data from quantum processes may plausibly offer these circumstances, while classical datasets may offer fewer opportunities. This is a qualified account of potential advantage, not a general speedup claim.
neurips-2021-the-inductive-bias-of-quant.tldr: Quantum-kernel advantages depend on suitable problem-specific inductive bias, with large feature spaces alone offering no guarantee.

paragraphs: Visual attention models often divide images into predefined patches and process many resulting tokens. TokenLearner instead learns to extract a small number of important tokens from the visual input. The representation is adaptive, allowing token selection to respond to the content rather than being fixed by a hand-designed partition.

Using fewer meaningful tokens makes it possible to model pairwise attention efficiently. For video, this supports reasoning across a longer temporal span; for images, it supports attention over spatial content. The method therefore changes how visual information is packaged before attention, making the selection of that information part of representation learning itself.

Experiments demonstrate strong performance on challenging video-recognition benchmarks and competitive results at significantly lower computational cost. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, Charades, and AViD. These findings support the value of adaptive tokenization for video understanding, while the proposed representation also applies to images. The key result is that a handful of learned tokens can support effective visual reasoning in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-tokenlearner-adaptive-space.tldr: TokenLearner adaptively extracts a few visual tokens, supporting strong video recognition with significantly reduced computation.

paragraphs: When test data differs from training data, a model may benefit from declining to predict on some examples. This paper studies abstention with a fixed cost. Its algorithm is transductive: it receives labeled training examples and the unlabeled test examples together before deciding which predictions to make.

The resulting prediction-loss guarantees match standard generalization bounds when test examples are independently drawn from the training distribution. Under shift, the bounds add a term equal to the abstention cost multiplied by a statistical measure of distribution mismatch, or by the fraction of adversarial examples. This explicitly relates the cost of handling unfamiliar data to the extent of the shift.

The paper also gives computational implementations for two learning settings. Linear regression admits a polynomial-time algorithm based on Celis-Dennis-Tapia optimization methods. Binary classification can be implemented efficiently using a proper agnostic learner, described as an empirical risk minimizer for the relevant class. The contribution ties optimal loss guarantees to concrete procedures for balancing prediction against paid abstention.
neurips-2021-towards-optimally-abstainin.tldr: A transductive abstention method provides optimal loss guarantees that account explicitly for distribution shift and the cost of declining predictions.

paragraphs: Selective rationalization explains predictions by choosing a small subset of input features sufficient for a predictor. A common design jointly trains a rationale generator and a predictor that sees only the selected features. This paper identifies a failure mode called interlocking: the predictor adapts to poor selections and reinforces them.

The authors trace this problem to concavity of the training objective with respect to the generator's selection policy. Their A2R framework adds another predictor driven by soft attention. The generator now supplies hard selections to the original predictor and soft attention to the added predictor, while also minimizing a gap between their predictions.

The additional predictor has a more favorable convexity property, and the theoretical analysis shows how A2R can overcome the concavity barrier. Experiments on two synthetic benchmarks and two real datasets show substantial alleviation of interlocking and explanations that agree better with human judgments. The result targets a specific feedback problem in joint training, helping rationale generation escape selections that the original predictor has learned to accommodate.
neurips-2021-understanding-interlocking-.tldr: A2R adds a soft-attention predictor to reduce self-reinforcing poor rationale selections and improve agreement with human judgments.

paragraphs: Affine-coupling normalizing flows are generative models whose structure makes likelihood computation efficient. Earlier universal-approximation results showed broad expressive power, but relied on transformations with nearly singular Jacobians. Such poor conditioning obstructs likelihood-based training, leaving open whether expressive approximation is possible while keeping the transformation well conditioned.

This paper proves that any log-concave distribution can be approximated using well-conditioned affine-coupling flows. The proof connects these architectures to underdamped Langevin dynamics and Hénon maps. Those connections provide a way to reason about both the distribution being represented and the conditioning of the transformation used to represent it.

The construction approximates a version of the target distribution padded with independent Gaussian variables. Earlier empirical work had observed that this padding improved conditioning, and the paper supplies theoretical support for that observation. The result therefore establishes a well-conditioned approximation guarantee for a specific distribution class and gives a mathematical basis for Gaussian padding. It does not extend that stated guarantee to every possible target distribution.
neurips-2021-universal-approximation-usi.tldr: Well-conditioned affine-coupling flows can approximate log-concave distributions, with the proof providing theoretical support for Gaussian padding.
